### Problem: Zero Remainder Array {#sec-gcd-p4-zeromod}

::: {.p-statement}
**Spend a rising counter to zero every remainder.** You start with `x = 0`. In one move you
either add the *current* `x` to exactly one still-unused array element and then do `x += 1`,
or you just do `x += 1`. Each element may be chosen at most once. Find the minimum number of
moves so that every element is divisible by `k`. Answer `t` independent test cases.

```text
n=4, k=3,  a=[1, 2, 1, 3]              -> 6
n=5, k=10, a=[20, 100, 50, 20, 100500] -> 0
n=8, k=8,  a=[1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8]  -> 8
```

For `a = [1, 2, 1, 3]`, `k = 3`: the two `1`s need `x \equiv 2 \pmod 3` and the `2` needs
`x \equiv 1 \pmod 3`. You can hand out `x = 1` (fixes the `2`), then the first `1` is fixed
at `x = 2`, and the second `1` must wait a whole cycle for `x = 5`. The last increment is
spent at `x = 5`, so you make `6` moves (`x` climbs to `6`).

**Constraints.** $1 \le n \le 2 \cdot 10^5$; $1 \le k \le 10^9$; $1 \le a_i \le 10^9$; the
sum of $n$ over test cases is at most $2 \cdot 10^5$.
Source: [CF 1374D · Zero Remainder Array](https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/1374/D){.solved rating="1400"}
:::

::: {.p-intuition}
Only the residue $r = a_i \bmod k$ matters, exactly as in @sec-gcd-p4-balance - but here an
element with residue $r > 0$ is fixed by *any* $x \equiv (k - r) \pmod k$, and $x$ only ever
increases by one per move. So all elements that want the same residue class $d = k - r$ are
served at $x = d,\, d + k,\, d + 2k, \ldots$ - a family of $\mathit{cnt}[d]$ elements costs
its last member $(\mathit{cnt}[d] - 1)\cdot k + d$ moves. The answer is the largest such
value over all classes, **plus one** because after the final element is served `x` still
increments. This is the residue histogram of @sec-gcd-a3 pushed to its counting conclusion.
:::

::: {.p-approach}
1. **Simulate the counter.** Walk $x = 0, 1, 2, \ldots$ and whenever some unserved element
   wants $x \bmod k$, spend $x$ on it. Stop when none remain; the number of steps is the
   answer. Faithful to the two operations, but $O(\text{answer})$ pseudo-polynomial.
2. **Count by residue class.** Bucket elements by $d = (k - a_i \bmod k) \bmod k$, then
   $\text{answer} = \max_d [(\mathit{cnt}[d] - 1)\cdot k + d] + 1$ (or $0$ if nothing needs
   serving). $O(n)$ with a hash map.
:::

::: {#fig-gcd-p4-zeromod}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    V.grid(ax, p, [["a[i]",   "1", "2", "1", "3"],
                   ["a mod 3", "1", "2", "1", "0"],
                   ["wants x", "2", "1", "2", "-"]],
           colors={(2, 1): "amber", (2, 3): "amber"}, cell_w=1.2)
V.show(draw)
```

Two elements want the same class $x \equiv 2 \pmod 3$ (amber). They cannot share an `x`, so
the second waits a full cycle - it is served at $x = 5$ while the first gets $x = 2$. The
largest `x` ever spent is $5$, hence $6$ moves.

:::

::: {.panel-tabset .solution-forms}

#### Walk the counter until nothing remains

::: {.form-next}
Do exactly what the statement says: raise `x` one at a time and, whenever an unserved
element is made divisible by adding the current `x`, spend `x` on it and mark it done. The
loop stops when every element is served; the number of `x`-increments is the answer. This
is $O(\text{answer})$ - fine to reason with, far too slow to submit when $k$ is large.
:::

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}

##### Python

```{python}
def zm_sim(a, k):
    need = [(k - x % k) % k for x in a if x % k != 0]   # each wants x % k == this
    remaining = list(need)
    x = 0
    while remaining:
        if x % k in remaining:
            remaining.remove(x % k)                     # spend this x on one element
        x += 1
    return x

assert zm_sim([1, 2, 1, 3], 3) == 6
assert zm_sim([20, 100, 50, 20, 100500], 10) == 0
assert zm_sim([1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8], 8) == 8
assert zm_sim([24] * 10, 25) == 227
```

##### C++

```cpp
long long zmSim(vector<long long>& a, long long k) {
    vector<long long> remaining;
    for (long long v : a)
        if (v % k != 0) remaining.push_back((k - v % k) % k);
    long long x = 0;
    while (!remaining.empty()) {
        for (size_t j = 0; j < remaining.size(); ++j)
            if (remaining[j] == x % k) { remaining.erase(remaining.begin() + j); break; }
        ++x;
    }
    return x;
}
```

:::

#### Count each residue class, take the last slot

::: {.form-next}
Group elements by $d = (k - a_i \bmod k) \bmod k$. The $\mathit{cnt}[d]$ elements of one
class are served at $x = d, d+k, \ldots, d + (\mathit{cnt}[d]-1)k$, so the last of them
costs $(\mathit{cnt}[d]-1)k + d$. Take the maximum over all classes and add one for the
final `x`-increment. $O(n)$.
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    title, inp, steps, final = Traces.get("zeromod", "formula")
    assert str(final) == "6"
    V.story(ax, p, title, inp, steps, final)
V.show(draw)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}

##### Python

```{python}
def zm_moves(a, k):
    need = {}
    for x in a:
        r = x % k
        if r:
            d = k - r
            need[d] = need.get(d, 0) + 1
    if not need:
        return 0
    best = max((cnt - 1) * k + d for d, cnt in need.items())
    return best + 1

assert zm_moves([1, 2, 1, 3], 3) == 6
assert zm_moves([8, 7, 1, 8, 3, 7, 5, 10, 8, 9], 6) == 18
assert zm_moves([20, 100, 50, 20, 100500], 10) == 0
assert zm_moves([24] * 10, 25) == 227
assert zm_moves([1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8], 8) == 8
for _ in range(120):
    a = [random.randint(1, 40) for _ in range(random.randint(1, 7))]
    k = random.randint(2, 9)
    assert zm_moves(a, k) == zm_sim(a, k), (a, k)
```

##### C++

```cpp
long long zmMoves(vector<long long>& a, long long k) {
    unordered_map<long long, long long> need;
    for (long long v : a) {
        long long r = v % k;
        if (r) need[k - r]++;
    }
    long long best = -1;
    for (auto& kv : need) {
        long long d = kv.first, cnt = kv.second;
        best = max(best, (cnt - 1) * k + d);
    }
    return best < 0 ? 0 : best + 1;
}
```

:::

:::

::: {.p-complexity}
**Time.** Rung 1 is $O(k \cdot \text{answer})$ in the worst case (pseudo-polynomial - never
submit it); rung 2 is $O(n)$ per test case. **Space.** $O(n)$ for the residue map. Watch the
overflow: $(\mathit{cnt}-1)\cdot k + d$ reaches $\approx 2 \cdot 10^{14}$, so use 64-bit
integers.
:::

::: {.p-edge}
- **Already divisible.** If every $a_i \equiv 0 \pmod k$ the map is empty and the answer is
  $0$ moves - do not add the `+1` in that case.
- **One huge class.** `a = [24]*10, k = 25`: all ten need $d = 1$, so the last is served at
  $(10-1)\cdot 25 + 1 = 226$ and the answer is $227$.
- **$k$ larger than every element.** Then $d = k - a_i$ values are all distinct, so the
  answer is $\max_i (k - a_i) + 1$.

**Debug tip.** The classic off-by-one here is forgetting the final `+1`: `best` is the
*largest `x` you spend*, but that move still increments `x`, so moves $=$ `best + 1` -
*unless* nothing ever needed an increment, in which case the answer is `0`.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistakes"}
- Reporting `max_d[(cnt-1)*k + d]` as the answer without the `+1`. That value is the last
  `x` you hand out; the move that hands it out also advances `x`, so you need one more.
- Applying the `+1` even when the array is *already* all-zero-mod-`k`; an empty need map is
  genuinely $0$ moves.
- Bucketing by $a_i \bmod k$ directly instead of by the increment $d = k - (a_i \bmod k)$
  the element actually waits for.
:::

**Variants.** @sec-gcd-p4-balance is the same residue-histogram idea over $\bmod 3$ where
surplus simply cycles forward; @sec-gcd-a3 develops the residue-counting that both problems use,
and explains why only $a_i \bmod k$ is ever read.
